questions.q: What kind of join does $lookup perform?
options: A left outer join against another collection in the same database
An inner join only
A cross join, matching every document against every other document
$lookup doesn't perform a join — it only renames fields
questions.explain: $lookup is documented as performing a left outer join, attaching matched documents from the foreign collection as an array field.

questions.q: Why does $lookup's output field come back as an array even when exactly one matching document exists?
options: Because $lookup is fundamentally a one-to-many join under the hood, regardless of how many documents actually match
It's a bug that MongoDB has never fixed
Arrays are required for all fields in a document, by BSON rules
It only returns an array if you explicitly request one
questions.explain: The guide explains $lookup always attaches matches as an array; a single match still means an array with one element, often flattened afterward with $unwind.

questions.q: In a $group stage, what role does the `_id` field play?
options: It defines the grouping key — the expression documents are grouped by, equivalent to a GROUP BY column list
It always refers to the document's original _id field and cannot be changed
It names the output collection
It sets the sort order of the results
questions.explain: Despite sharing a name with the document field, _id inside $group specifies the grouping key/expression, not necessarily the original _id.

questions.q: What does $facet let you do that separate $match/$group pipelines can't do as efficiently?
options: Run multiple independent sub-pipelines against the same input documents in a single pass, returning each result set under its own key
Perform joins across three or more collections at once
Automatically create indexes on frequently queried fields
Convert BSON documents into relational tables permanently
questions.explain: $facet computes multiple aggregation results (e.g. a breakdown and a top-N list) from one pass over the input, rather than requiring separate queries.

questions.q: Which accumulator operators are used inside $group, and what SQL constructs do they correspond to?
options: $sum, $avg, $count, $min, $max — equivalent to SUM(), AVG(), COUNT(), MIN(), MAX() in SQL
$match, $sort, $limit — equivalent to WHERE, ORDER BY, TOP
$lookup, $unwind — equivalent to JOIN and UNNEST
$project, $addFields — equivalent to computed columns
questions.explain: $sum, $avg, $count, $min, and $max are the accumulator operators used inside $group, directly mapping to SQL's aggregate functions.
